children: Stocks and bonds swooned yesterday after the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates for the first time in three years-only to reverse course and charge higher in premarket trading this morning. Why the quick turnaround?
One explanation, according to Mohit Kumar, Jefferies' chief European economist: Investors realize they may have overreacted to Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's hawkish tone.

"I don't think Warsh indicated a series of rate hikes," Kumar said. "The market reaction today feels like a repricing to the scenario that the Fed will likely hike, but not deliver three, which are currently priced in."

LSEG data show that traders are currently pricing in three more quarter-point rate increases over the next 12 months. But Kumar notes that the Fed's so-called dot plot-which central-bank officials use to guide on their outlook for rates-isn't quite so severe. Yesterday's dot plot showed a median forecast of one more rate increase this year.
As for 2027? The median official saw rates holding steady. (That being said, it's worth noting that eight out of 18 participating officials saw one more rate hike next year.)
Also adding to sentiment today, Kumar noted: Lower oil prices, which are offering a reprieve for investors who have grown increasingly worried about their impact on inflation.
